questions.question: What does pairing <label for="email"> with <input id="email"> provide that placeholder text does not?
options: Nothing meaningfully different — placeholders are an equivalent substitute
Clicking the label focuses the input (a larger tap target), and screen readers announce the label when the input receives focus
It makes the input submit automatically
It is only useful for styling purposes
questions.explanation: Placeholder text disappears once typing starts and isn't reliably announced the same way; a properly associated label persists and is read by assistive technology on focus.

questions.question: Why does <fieldset>/<legend> matter for a group of radio buttons specifically?
options: It changes how the radio buttons are submitted to the server
It lets a screen reader announce the group's purpose and count (e.g. 'Shipping method, group of 3') instead of three unrelated inputs
It is purely a visual border with no accessibility effect
It is required for radio buttons to function at all
questions.explanation: Without fieldset/legend, a screen reader has no indication that the radio inputs are related choices within a single question.

questions.question: Beyond triggering the right mobile keyboard, what else does choosing `type="email"` over `type="text"` give you for free?
options: Built-in browser validation that rejects a value without an @ on form submission, with no JavaScript required
Automatic translation of the input value
It has no functional difference from type="text"
questions.explanation: Type-specific native validation (email format, number ranges, etc.) runs on submission automatically, independent of any JavaScript.

questions.question: Why would a form still need JavaScript validation even after using required/pattern/minlength attributes?
options: Native validation attributes don't actually work in any browser
Native validation can't express cross-field rules (like matching two password fields) or custom-styled error messages, and can't perform async checks like a uniqueness lookup
JavaScript validation is required by HTML5 specification
Using both is redundant and one should always be removed
questions.explanation: Native attributes are a good first line of defense but have real limits — cross-field validation, custom error UI, and async checks all require JavaScript.
